system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

**Significance (p. 30).** States a governing rule of the entire system: every scale can be entered at any internal note, and all scales can be chained in any order, giving the player maximum flexibility in approaching a tonal center.

**Significance (p. 31).** Identifies Scale #14 as a pentatonic and maps each of its five notes to their harmonic function within the V chord and F major, providing the template for understanding melodic function in the system.

## No wrong notes doctrine

> There are no wrong notes when
> factors such as fixation on a key center, Vantage
>
> Point, Interval Tonics, Resolution are considered
>
> along with a certain Confidence within the artist
> himself. The entire chromatic scale is at our
> disposal thanks to Great Nature.

**Significance (p. 31).** Articulates the foundational rule of the method -- that chromaticism is valid when governed by key-center fixation, vantage point, interval tonics, resolution, and confident intent -- listing the exact conditions that make any note acceptable.

## Scale #16 major with raised 4th

> This scale, is a major scale with a raised 4th
> in it. The 4th is the major 3rd of the V chord,
> also the scale begins on the 7th of the V chord
> of F major making a complete E-B b ceneans. The
> EM chord is produced by another mode of this
> scale (major) on its 7th degree so it naturally
> leads into F major. The last note of this scale
> is "rocked" back from its last note pb to A the
> important major 3rd of F major.

**Significance (p. 33).** Defines Scale #16 as a Lydian-type (major + raised 4th) and explains three convergence mechanisms: the E-Bb tritone, the EM chord generated on the 7th modal degree, and the terminal pitch 'rocked' to the major 3rd of F.

## 360-degree key-center system defined

> You might call this system the astrological charting of a key
>
> center because the 360° circle is used & the key center lies
>
> at the middle which represents the person or key acted upon.
>
> You are bombarding this person, or in this case key center
>
> with 24 scales & their constituent chords.

**Significance (p. 33).** Names and conceptualizes the overall architecture of the method -- 24 scales orbiting a single tonal center at 360 degrees -- giving the student a mental model for how all the scales relate to each other and to F major.

## Scale #17 Spanish scale, tension-relaxation

> This scale of mine has a different quality in that
> it is a spanish sounding scale embodying vital
> motes of the F & ebtonality causing a tension
> relaxation feeling all under one roof, It begins
> on the note F & ends on F, our desired tonal
> destination.

**Significance (p. 34).** Introduces the Spanish-quality scale as a distinct color in the system and identifies its key structural feature: it embodies both F and E-flat tonality simultaneously, creating tension-relaxation within a single scale.

## Scale #18 melodic minor tetrachords

> It is an F minor

> of FA 9th chord). The lst tetrachord is F
> minor & the last tetrachord (C D E F) is F major.
> This denotes minor & major color under one roof
> of the same tonality.

**Significance (p. 35).** Defines Scale #18's construction as melodic minor by naming its two tetrachords -- F minor then F major -- and explains how the dual-color architecture produces convergent motion toward F major.

**Significance (p. 35).** Demonstrates a key analytical technique of the method -- reading a single pitch (Ab) simultaneously as a scale-degree in the tonic minor and as the +5 of the dominant chord -- illustrating how dual harmonic identity justifies chromatic notes.
